overview.text: David Herbert Lawrence (1885–1930) was an English novelist, poet, short-story writer, essayist, and playwright, born in Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, to a coal-mining family. His first published works were poems, but he became best known for novels including Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow, Women in Love, and Lady Chatterley’s Lover. His writing is distinctive for its attention to bodily and emotional experience, nature, and the conflict he saw between human vitality and modern industrial society. His treatments of sexuality and challenges to social convention made his work controversial; Lady Chatterley’s Lover was privately printed in 1928 and became a focus of censorship disputes. His early poetry shows Imagist influence, though he chose an independent path.

key_facts.text: Lawrence was born in Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, on September 11, 1885, and died in France on March 2, 1930.
His father was a coal miner; Lawrence’s working-class origins informed his background as an English writer.
His early poems were influenced by Ezra Pound and Imagism, but Lawrence pursued an independent course.
Among his major novels are Sons and Lovers, The Rainbow, Women in Love, and Lady Chatterley’s Lover.
Lady Chatterley’s Lover was privately printed in 1928 and became especially associated with censorship controversy.
